content: Cocamidopropyl betaine (CAPB) is a zwitterionic surfactant that contains a quaternary ammonium cation within its molecular structure. It appears as a viscous, pale yellow, transparent liquid. CAPB is commonly used as a surfactant in bath products such as shampoos and hand soaps. It also functions as an emulsifying agent and thickener in cosmetics, and it helps to reduce the irritation that purely ionic surfactants can cause. Additionally, it acts as an antistatic agent in hair conditioners. Cocamidopropyl betaine is synthesized from cocamide and betaine. The length of the carbon chain in the molecule is discussed under cocamide. CAPB is considered a medium-strength surfactant and is generally non-irritating to the skin and mucous membranes. However, some studies have identified it as a potential allergen. CAPB also exhibits antiseptic properties, making it suitable for use in personal hygiene products. It is compatible with cationic, anionic, and nonionic surfactants. Over time, CAPB has largely replaced cocamide DEA in many formulations. CAPB is typically available as an aqueous solution with a concentration of approximately 30%. It contains less than 3% glycerol and less than 15 ppm of dimethylaminopropylamine (DMAPA). However, some commercial grades may contain up to 3% amidoamine (AA). The impurities AA and DMAPA are of particular concern, as they have been implicated in causing skin sensitization reactions. These by-products can be minimized by using a moderate excess of chloroacetate and carefully adjusting the pH during the betainization reaction, accompanied by regular analytical monitoring. There are safety concerns regarding CAPB, as it has been reported to cause allergic reactions in some individuals. However, a controlled pilot study suggests that these cases may represent irritant reactions rather than true allergic responses. Human studies have demonstrated that CAPB has a low sensitizing potential when the levels of impurities such as amidoamine (AA) and dimethylaminopropylamine (DMAPA) are kept low and tightly controlled. Other studies have concluded that most apparent allergic reactions to CAPB are more likely attributable to amidoamine rather than CAPB itself.
